name: Stephen I of Hungary
title: King of Hungary

epithets.name: the Saint
epithets.note: Canonised on 20 August 1083 together with his son Emeric; the day is still Hungary’s foundation feast.

summary: First crowned king of Hungary, who founded its church and its county system, issued its first written laws, and was canonised in 1083 as the kingdom’s patron saint.
details: Stephen inherited the rule of the Magyars from his father Géza in 997 and spent forty years converting a steppe confederation into a Christian kingdom with counties, bishoprics, coinage and written law. His only surviving son died before him, and the succession he arranged collapsed within three years of his death.
overview: Stephen I was the first crowned king of Hungary and the man who turned a confederation of Magyar clans into a Latin Christian kingdom. greatestFeats: Crowned first king of Hungary at the turn of the year 1000
Founded the archbishopric of Esztergom and the Hungarian bishoprics
Built the county system of royal fortresses under an ispán
Issued Hungary’s first written law codes and the Admonitions to his son

birth.note: Born Vajk, son of Grand Prince Géza and Sarolt, daughter of the Transylvanian chieftain Gyula; the year is not securely recorded and some accounts place it as early as 969.

death.circumstance: Died after years of illness and was buried in the basilica he had built at Székesfehérvár, which became the coronation and burial church of the Hungarian kings.

quickFacts.knownFor: Founding the Christian kingdom of Hungary, its counties and its church

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Stephen I was the first crowned king of Hungary and the man who turned a confederation of Magyar clans into a Latin Christian kingdom. Born Vajk, the son of Grand Prince Géza, he succeeded his father in 997, put down the claim of his kinsman Koppány, and was crowned at the turn of the year 1000 with a crown that Hungarian tradition says came from Pope Silvester II.

In a reign of nearly forty years he built the framework the kingdom kept for centuries: royal fortresses with a county around each of them, an archbishopric at Esztergom with bishoprics under it, monasteries at Pannonhalma and elsewhere, two books of written law, and a pilgrim road across Hungary to Jerusalem. He outlived his son Emeric, broke with the kinsman who should have followed him, died on 15 August 1038 and was canonised in 1083.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: He was born at Esztergom about 975 and named Vajk, a name of Turkic origin. His father Géza was grand prince of the Hungarians, the ruler of a confederation that had raided Latin Europe for two generations and had been stopped at the Lech in 955; his mother Sarolt was the daughter of the Gyula of Transylvania and had been baptised in the Byzantine rite. Géza accepted Western missionaries, was baptised himself, and — in the judgement of nearly every source that describes him — went on sacrificing to the old gods as well.

Vajk was baptised Stephen, probably by or in the presence of Adalbert of Prague, and was married about 996 to Gisela of Bavaria, sister of the future emperor Henry II. The marriage brought German knights, clerics and craftsmen into Hungary and tied the dynasty to the Ottonian house, which mattered immediately: when Géza died in 997 those knights fought for his son.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Almost everything written about Stephen’s character was written to make a saint. Three legends compiled between about 1080 and 1116 — the Greater and Lesser Legends and the version by Bishop Hartvik — supply the piety, the alms, the night visits to the poor and the crown sent from Rome, and they are hagiography before they are biography. The Illuminated Chronicle, two and a half centuries later, adds the drama of the campaigns. None of these is a neutral witness, and the earliest of them was produced for the canonisation itself.

Two documents come closer to the man. The law codes are blunt, practical and severe: they fine the man who mutters in church, enforce Sunday observance, protect the property of widows and the freedom of slaves manumitted before witnesses, and mutilate thieves. The Admonitions written in his name for his son Emeric are the closest thing to a voice, and their most famous passage is a piece of political advice rather than devotion — that a kingdom of one language and one custom is weak and fragile, and that a king should honour the strangers who come to him, because they bring their skills with them.

Against the saint stands the treatment of his own kin. Koppány was killed and his body quartered and displayed at four fortresses as a warning; his cousin Vazul, the obvious adult heir, was blinded and his ears filled with molten lead, according to the chronicles, and Vazul’s sons were driven into exile. Modern historians — Gyula Kristó, Pál Engel and Nora Berend among them — treat that severity as inseparable from the achievement rather than as a stain on it: a ruler imposing an unfamiliar religion and an unfamiliar form of authority on a society organised by kinship had no gentle instruments, and Stephen used the ones he had without visible hesitation.

contentSections.title: Koppány and the fight for the succession
paragraphs: Géza died in 997 having designated his son, which broke with the Magyar custom of seniority — succession by the eldest male of the ruling kindred. That custom had a claimant ready in Koppány, lord of Somogy and a member of the Árpád line, who demanded both the rule and, by the old right, Géza’s widow Sarolt.

Stephen met him in 997 or 998 in the country near Veszprém, at the head of a force that combined his own retainers with the German heavy cavalry that had come with Gisela, commanded by Vecelin. Koppány was killed in the fighting. His body was cut into four and fixed to the gates of the fortresses at Esztergom, Győr, Veszprém and Gyulafehérvár — a message addressed to everyone who preferred the old arrangement, and the beginning of the tithe of Somogy granted to the abbey of Pannonhalma.

contentSections.title: The crown of 1000 and what is tradition
paragraphs: Stephen was crowned at the turn of the year 1000, most often dated to 25 December 1000 or 1 January 1001; some German scholarship prefers August 1000. The coronation made Hungary a kingdom rather than a principality and placed it inside Latin Christendom rather than in the Byzantine sphere his mother’s family had known.

The famous part of the story is the crown itself. Bishop Hartvik, writing about 1116, says that Pope Silvester II had a crown prepared for the Polish duke, was told in a vision to give it to the envoys of the Hungarians instead, and sent it with a letter granting Stephen apostolic authority over his church. No papal record of any such grant survives, the legend was written a century after the event and served a specific purpose in the investiture quarrel, and modern historians divide over how much of it to keep: some argue for a genuine papal recognition arranged with the consent of Emperor Otto III, others for an imperial crown and a papal blessing, and Hungarian scholarship generally treats Stephen’s own charters — dated by his regnal years and declaring him to rule by the will of God, never by imperial grant — as the better evidence of what he claimed.

What the tradition certainly is not is the history of the object now called the Holy Crown of Hungary. Every part of that crown has been dated later than Stephen: the lower band is Byzantine work of the 1070s naming Michael VII Doukas and Géza I, and the upper bands were joined to it later still. It is the crown of the Hungarian kingship, but it was never on Stephen’s head.

contentSections.title: Counties, ispáns and royal government
paragraphs: The framework Stephen built rested on fortresses. He took the lands of defeated rivals into royal hands, garrisoned a castle at the centre of each district, and appointed an ispán — a count answerable to him alone — to command its troops, hold its court and collect its revenues, keeping a third of them and sending two thirds to the king. Roughly forty of these comitatus, the vármegye of later Hungarian usage, covered the kingdom by the end of the reign.

The effect was to cut across the kinship structure that had organised Magyar society. Authority now followed territory and royal appointment rather than descent within a clan, and the ispán held office at the king’s pleasure rather than by inheritance. Stephen paired it with a silver coinage struck with his name, the palatine and the royal court as a judicial centre, and the settlement of foreign knights, priests and craftsmen on royal land. The counties outlasted the dynasty, the medieval kingdom and the Ottoman conquest, and were still the administrative skeleton of Hungary in the nineteenth century.

contentSections.title: The church he founded
paragraphs: Stephen created a church province in a generation. Esztergom became the archbishopric and its holder the primate of Hungary; Kalocsa followed as a second metropolitan see; and bishoprics were established at Veszprém, Győr, Pécs in 1009, Eger, Gyulafehérvár in Transylvania and Csanád in 1030, the last of them for Gerard, the Venetian monk who became the country’s best-known martyr. A law required every ten villages to build a church and endow it, with the king supplying the vestments and books and the bishop the priest.

The monasteries came with the same deliberation. Pannonhalma, begun under Géza, received its charter from Stephen in 1002 with the tithe of Somogy; Pécsvárad, Zalavár and Bakonybél followed. Beyond his own borders he endowed hospices for Hungarian pilgrims at Rome, Ravenna, Constantinople and Jerusalem, and opened the overland pilgrim route through Hungary that western travellers used for the rest of the Middle Ages — a piece of infrastructure that did as much for the kingdom’s standing in Latin Europe as any of his wars.

contentSections.title: Laws, the Admonitions and the frontiers
paragraphs: Two books of laws survive in Stephen’s name, the first from early in the reign and the second possibly from after 1031. They legislate for a society being remade: attendance at Sunday mass, confession before death, the inviolability of church property, the status of freedmen, the punishment of perjury, theft and murder, and — repeatedly — the protection of royal revenue. They are the earliest written law of the Hungarian kingdom and the best single source for what its ruler was actually trying to change.

The Admonitions, the Libellus de institutione morum addressed to his son Emeric, belong to the European genre of advice to princes but read as a specific brief for a new and mixed kingdom: keep the faith, respect the bishops and the counsellors, judge patiently, and welcome incomers rather than fear them.

The frontiers were secured piecemeal. Stephen took Transylvania from his maternal uncle Gyula in 1003 and defeated Kean, a chieftain in the south; he fought the Pechenegs on the eastern edge and campaigned with Byzantine forces against Bulgaria in 1018; and when Conrad II invaded in 1030 he answered by withdrawing before the German army, emptying the country in its path and letting hunger do the work, so that the emperor retreated and the peace of 1031 confirmed Hungary’s border on the Leitha.

contentSections.title: Emeric, Vazul and a broken succession
paragraphs: Everything Stephen built assumed an heir he had trained. Emeric — the son the Admonitions were written for — was killed by a boar while hunting in 1031, and the chronicles date the king’s decline from that day.

The obvious successor by the old custom was his cousin Vazul, a grown man of the Árpád line, but Vazul was a doubtful Christian and, in the chronicles’ account, was blinded and deafened with molten lead while Stephen lay ill, with Stephen’s consent or at least without his prevention; Vazul’s three sons Levente, Andrew and Béla fled the country. In their place Stephen named Peter Orseolo, the son of his sister and the doge of Venice.

The arrangement lasted three years. Peter’s favour to his foreign followers provoked a rising that deposed him in 1041, and after his brief restoration and a pagan revolt the crown went in 1046 to Andrew, one of the exiled sons of the man Stephen had blinded. The dynasty survived through the branch he tried to exclude.

contentSections.title: Death and canonisation
paragraphs: Stephen died on 15 August 1038, the feast of the Assumption, and was buried in the marble sarcophagus in the basilica he had raised at Székesfehérvár. Hungarian tradition holds that he offered the kingdom to the Virgin before his death, and the Regnum Marianum, the Marian kingdom, became a lasting idea in Hungarian political religion.

Forty-five years later Ladislaus I, needing a sanctified founder for a kingdom that had been through civil war and German intervention, obtained the canonisation of Stephen together with Emeric and Bishop Gerard. The remains were raised on 20 August 1083, and the right hand found incorrupt became the Holy Right, still carried in procession in Budapest on that date. The canonisation was a political act as well as a religious one, and it fixed Stephen permanently as the kingdom’s founder rather than one strong ruler among several.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: The institutions held. Later Árpád kings ruled through the counties Stephen laid out and the bishoprics he endowed, and the law of the kingdom dated itself from his codes; when Andrew II of Hungary conceded the Golden Bull in 1222 and when Béla IV of Hungary rebuilt after the Mongol invasion, both worked with the structure Stephen had set rather than replacing it.

His memory has been claimed by every later Hungarian regime that needed a founder, which is its own kind of distortion: the figure who appears on nineteenth-century monuments and modern coins is a national symbol built out of the eleventh-century legends. The eleventh-century evidence is narrower and harder — charters, coins, two law books and a ruined basilica — and it shows a ruler who imposed a church, a fiscal system and a written law on a society that had none of the three, and made them stick.

keyAchievements.title: Crowned first king of Hungary
keyAchievements.description: The coronation at the turn of the year 1000 made Hungary a Latin Christian kingdom rather than a steppe principality.

keyAchievements.title: The county system
keyAchievements.description: Roughly forty royal fortresses, each with an ispán answerable to the king, replaced clan authority with territorial government.

keyAchievements.title: The Hungarian church
keyAchievements.description: Esztergom and Kalocsa as archbishoprics, bishoprics from Pécs to Csanád, and the abbeys of Pannonhalma, Pécsvárad, Zalavár and Bakonybél.

keyAchievements.title: Written law and the Admonitions
keyAchievements.description: Two books of laws and the advice text for his son Emeric, the earliest Hungarian legal and political writing.

timeline.title: Born at Esztergom
timeline.description: Born Vajk to Grand Prince Géza and Sarolt, and baptised Stephen in childhood.

timeline.title: Succeeds Géza
timeline.description: Took the rule of the Hungarians on his father’s death, by designation rather than by the seniority custom.

timeline.title: Defeats Koppány
timeline.description: Beat his kinsman’s claim in the country near Veszprém with German knights brought by Gisela of Bavaria; Koppány was killed and quartered.

timeline.title: Crowned king of Hungary
timeline.description: Crowned at the turn of the year with a crown that Hartvik’s legend, written a century later, says Pope Silvester II sent.

timeline.title: Charter for Pannonhalma
timeline.description: Confirmed the Benedictine abbey with the tithe of Somogy, the earliest surviving Hungarian charter.

timeline.title: Takes Transylvania
timeline.description: Captured his maternal uncle Gyula and annexed his lands, later defeating the chieftain Kean in the south.

timeline.title: Opens the pilgrim road
timeline.description: Campaigned alongside Byzantine forces against Bulgaria and opened the overland route through Hungary to Jerusalem, endowing hospices along it.

timeline.title: Repels Conrad II
timeline.description: Withdrew before the imperial army and stripped the country in its path; the peace of 1031 fixed the western border on the Leitha.

timeline.title: Death of Emeric
timeline.description: His heir was killed by a boar while hunting, leaving the succession to a cousin he did not trust.

timeline.title: Died at Székesfehérvár
timeline.description: Buried in the basilica he built, which became the coronation and burial church of the Hungarian kings.

timeline.title: Canonised
timeline.description: Raised to the altars with his son Emeric and Bishop Gerard under Ladislaus I, giving the kingdom a sainted founder.

succession.note: Stephen ruled as grand prince from 997 and as king from the coronation of 1000/1001; the boxes show the kingship.

predecessor.note: The first crowned king. He had succeeded his father Géza as grand prince of the Hungarians in 997, three years before the coronation raised the office to a kingship.

successor.note: Son of his sister and the doge of Venice, named heir after Emeric’s death in 1031; king from 1038 until a rising deposed him in 1041.

people.title: Andrew II of Hungary
people.label: Later Árpád king who conceded the Golden Bull

people.title: Béla IV of Hungary
